q: At the drinking parties of one ancient civilisation the wine was mixed with water in a communal bowl before it went round, and taking it neat was thought the habit of barbarians. Which civilisation?
exp: The bowl was a krater and the proportions were argued over as a question of manners, with something like one part wine to three of water counted as civilised. Rome inherited the custom, which is why ancient descriptions of drinking bear so little relation to how a glass is poured now.

q: Vine growing survived the collapse of the western empire and pushed further north than Rome had ever taken it, carried by the religious houses. Which requirement kept it going?
opts: Church law obliged every abbey to be self-sufficient in all crops
Wine was the only lawful form in which a tithe could be paid
Wine was needed for the celebration of the Mass
Monks were forbidden by their rule to drink water
exp: A church without wine could not say Mass, so every religious house had reason to secure a supply it controlled rather than buying one. That is why vineyards appear in medieval England, in Poland and along the Baltic, at latitudes where the economics alone would never have justified them.

q: A sixth-century monastic rule granted each monk a daily measure of wine rather than forbidding it, and the houses that adopted it became vineyard owners across Europe. Whose rule was it?
exp: The rule concedes that wine is no drink for monks and then allows a daily ration anyway, on the grounds that the times will not bear the stricter line. That concession shaped a thousand years of European agriculture, and Bernard of Clairvaux belongs to the reforming order that grew out of it five centuries later.

q: Records of which parcels ripened first and which gave the best wine accumulated in monastic hands over centuries and almost nowhere else. Which feature of those houses accounts for it?
opts: They were literate corporate bodies that outlived any individual owner
They alone were permitted to own vineyards
Their wine was exempt from tax
exp: A monastery does not divide its land among heirs and does not forget what the previous generation learned, so observations could be written down and compared harvest after harvest. Secular holdings changed hands, were split and were fought over, and whatever they had learned went with them.

q: England had working vineyards attached to its abbeys until a sixteenth-century king broke with Rome and closed them, and commercial planting there did not resume in earnest for four centuries. Which event was that?
opts: The enclosure of the common fields
exp: Henry VIII's break with Rome removed both the institutions and the guaranteed market for their wine at a stroke. A cooling climate over the following centuries finished the job, and English vineyards returned as a serious business only in the later twentieth century.

q: Vineyards belonging to the French church were seized in the 1790s and auctioned to whoever could pay, which is how a great deal of the country's finest land first reached private hands. Which upheaval put it on the market?
exp: The confiscated estates were sold as biens nationaux, national property, and the buyers ranged from Paris merchants to the growers who had worked the ground for the monks. Several celebrated vineyards passed out of church ownership within a few years of one another, and none has returned.

q: A marriage in 1152 carried the duchy of Aquitaine to the future king of England, and for three hundred years afterwards Bordeaux shipped most of its wine to London. Whose marriage was it?
opts: Eleanor of Aquitaine to Henry Plantagenet
Catherine de Medici to Henry II of France
Mary of Guise to James V of Scotland
Anne of Brittany to Charles VIII
exp: Gascony became English territory and its wine entered England at preferential duty, which built the region's export trade centuries before anyone thought of ranking its estates. The political connection ended with the English defeat at Castillon in 1453; the London market for the wine never did.

q: English woollens were let into Portugal in 1703, and Portuguese wine came into England at a third less duty than French wine paid. Which treaty struck that bargain?
exp: It was signed while England was at war with France, so the gap in duty was as much politics as commerce, and the preference shaped British drinking for well over a century, until the duties on French and Portuguese wine were equalised in 1831 and the treaty lapsed a few years later. Generations of British drinkers grew up on Portuguese wine because it was the cheap option rather than the fashionable one.

q: Engineers from the Low Countries were hired in the seventeenth century to cut drainage channels through the marshes north of Bordeaux, uncovering the gravel banks that now carry its best vineyards. Which people did that work?
exp: They had drained their own country and sold the technique across northern Europe, and the channels they cut still drain the peninsula today. Before that work the region's reputation rested on the gravel south of the city, which had never needed draining.

q: A London diarist recorded in 1663 that he had drunk a French wine with a particular good taste of its own, and named the property rather than the region it came from. Whose diary was it?
exp: The wine came from Haut-Brion, and the entry marks the moment a single Bordeaux property began to be sold on its own name at a premium over its neighbours. Selling an estate rather than a district is the commercial idea everything later in fine wine is built on.

q: War with France in the 1690s shut French wine out of England behind punitive duty, and London merchants went looking up the Douro for something to sell instead. Which trade grew out of that search?
exp: Douro wine was rough and did not travel well, which is precisely why British firms established themselves on the river to solve the problem rather than simply buying from a broker. It is the reason so many of the great shipping names there are English or Scottish to this day.

q: An American minister to France spent the spring of 1787 touring vineyards from Burgundy to Bordeaux, took meticulous notes on owners and prices, and afterwards ordered his wine direct from the properties. Who was he?
exp: He wanted to know which slope made which wine and recorded what he found as a surveyor would. Buying direct from a property instead of through a merchant was unusual then, and it is the reason bottles claiming to bear his initials have caused so much argument among collectors since.

q: Popular history credits a Benedictine cellarer at Hautvillers with inventing sparkling Champagne. What did he actually spend his career doing?
opts: Blending across many parcels, and pressing black grapes for clear white wine
Devising the wire cage that holds a cork down
Discovering the second fermentation and learning to provoke it
exp: Bubbles were a fault in his day and his cellars worked hard to prevent them, since a bottle that refermented was as likely to burst as to please anyone. His lasting achievements were assemblage, building a wine from fruit grown on many different sites, and pressing dark-skinned grapes fast enough to keep the juice white.

q: Coal-fired furnaces in seventeenth-century England turned out glass darker, thicker and far stronger than the wood-fired French kind, which is what first made a wine under pressure worth keeping. Which Englishman is credited with the design?
exp: England had banned wood in glass furnaces to preserve timber for the navy, so its glassmakers had already moved to coal and were reaching higher temperatures than anyone else. A bottle of the softer continental glass burst readily under pressure, and cellars were still losing serious fractions of a vintage to breakage well into the nineteenth century.

q: A paper read to the Royal Society in 1662 described putting sugar into finished wine so that it would come out brisk and sparkling, decades before the practice is recorded in France. Who presented it?
exp: Merret was a physician and an early fellow of the society, and his note is the first written description of provoking a second fermentation on purpose. It is why the English claim on the technique is taken seriously by historians, whatever the marketing of the region that perfected it may suggest.

q: Bottles were blown squat and onion-shaped until the eighteenth century, when glassmakers began drawing them out into straight-sided cylinders. What did the new shape make possible?
opts: Storing them on their sides to age
Filling and corking them by machine at speed
exp: A cylinder stacks, and a cork kept wet by the wine does not shrink and let air past. The idea of a vintage worth keeping for years, and of a cellar as something with a value, follows directly from a change in the shape of the glass.
